title: Strategy and Template Method
scopeHtml: Scope: Strategy and Template Method patterns with before/after refactors, Java and Kotlin, library and Android examples, when not to use. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why behavioral patterns exist
notes.html:
Behavioral patterns are recipes for how objects divide work and talk to each other. Creational patterns say how objects are made, structural ones how they are assembled, behavioral ones how they behave together at runtime. Most of them attack one smell: a giant if/else or switch that keeps growing, or objects that know too much about each other.

The core trick behind almost all of them: replace a conditional with polymorphism, or replace a direct call with an indirection. Instead of "if type is A do this, else if B do that", you hold an object that already knows what to do.

Worked example. A checkout method has 6 payment branches, 40 lines each = 240 lines in one method. Each new payment type edits that method (risk of breaking the other 5). After a pattern: 6 classes of about 40 lines, adding a 7th touches zero existing lines. That is the Open/Closed Principle in numbers.

Industry examples. Java's Comparator (Strategy), RecyclerView.Adapter (Template-ish), LiveData (Observer), OkHttp interceptors (Chain of Responsibility), Android Intent handling and Handler messages (Command-like).

Everyday analogy. A restaurant: the waiter does not cook each dish personally with a giant rulebook; he hands the order to the right station.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting GoF names with no code. Always show a before and after.
  • Applying a pattern where one if is clearer. Patterns have a cost: more classes and more indirection.
  • Confusing look-alikes (Strategy vs State vs Command). The last note of this track compares them.

notes.title: Strategy: the idea
notes.html:
Strategy lets you pick an algorithm at runtime by putting each variant behind the same interface. The caller (the "context") holds a reference to a strategy and delegates. Change the object, change the behaviour, without touching the caller.

Use it when you have several ways to do one job: sort order, pricing rule, compression format, retry policy, route calculation.

+----------------+        +-------------------+
|  Checkout      |------->| <<interface>>     |
| (context)      |        | DiscountStrategy  |
| - strategy     |        | + apply(total)    |
| + pay(total)   |        +---------+---------+
+----------------+                  ^
        +---------------------------+------------------+
        |                           |                  |
 +--------------+          +----------------+  +----------------+
 | NoDiscount   |          | PercentOff     |  | FlatOff        |
 +--------------+          +----------------+  +----------------+

Before (the smell):

class Checkout {
    double pay(double total, String coupon) {
        if (coupon.equals("NONE"))        return total;
        else if (coupon.equals("PERCENT")) return total * 0.9;
        else if (coupon.equals("FLAT"))    return total - 100;
        else throw new IllegalArgumentException(coupon);
    }
}

Every new coupon edits pay. Tests must cover all branches in one method.

After:

interface DiscountStrategy { double apply(double total); }

class PercentOff implements DiscountStrategy {
    private final double pct;
    PercentOff(double pct) { this.pct = pct; }
    public double apply(double total) { return total * (1 - pct); }
}
class FlatOff implements DiscountStrategy {
    private final double amount;
    FlatOff(double amount) { this.amount = amount; }
    public double apply(double total) { return Math.max(0, total - amount); }
}

class Checkout {
    private DiscountStrategy strategy;
    Checkout(DiscountStrategy s) { this.strategy = s; }
    void setStrategy(DiscountStrategy s) { this.strategy = s; }
    double pay(double total) { return strategy.apply(total); }
}
// new Checkout(new PercentOff(0.10)).pay(1000) -> 900.0

Kotlin variant. A strategy with one method is just a function, so use a function type or fun interface:

fun interface DiscountStrategy { fun apply(total: Double): Double }

class Checkout(private var strategy: DiscountStrategy) {
    fun pay(total: Double) = strategy.apply(total)
}

val tenOff = DiscountStrategy { it * 0.9 }
val flat100 = DiscountStrategy { (it - 100).coerceAtLeast(0.0) }
println(Checkout(tenOff).pay(1000.0)) // 900.0

Decision gravity. Choosing Strategy is reversible and cheap: it is a local refactor behind an interface. The risky part is the interface shape; if two strategies need different inputs (one needs the user, one needs the cart), the interface grows or you pass a context object. Interface changes touch every implementation.

Everyday analogy. Choosing how to get to the airport: taxi, metro or bike. Same goal, interchangeable ways, you pick at departure.

Common interview traps.

  • Strategy vs a plain if: with two stable branches that never change, if is fine.
  • Passing the whole context to every strategy "just in case" couples them to the caller.
  • Who picks the strategy? Say it out loud: a factory, config, or the caller. Often a Map from key to strategy replaces the original if chain.

notes.title: Strategy in real libraries and Android
notes.html:
You already use Strategy daily:

Where Strategy interface Variants
Java collections Comparator<T> Comparator.comparing(...), reversed, custom
java.util.concurrent RejectedExecutionHandler Abort, CallerRuns, Discard
Android layouts RecyclerView.LayoutManager Linear, Grid, StaggeredGrid
Android image loading Glide/Coil Transformation, DiskCacheStrategy circle crop, none/all/automatic
OkHttp / Retrofit Converter.Factory Gson, Moshi, kotlinx.serialization
Spring Security PasswordEncoder BCrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2
Dependency injection Hilt-bound interface Real vs fake in tests

Worked example (retry policy). A client retries failed calls. Strategies: FixedDelay(500ms), ExponentialBackoff(base=200ms, factor=2, max=10s) and NoRetry. With exponential backoff: waits 200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200 ms for 5 attempts (about 6.2 s total). Add jitter (random +/-20%) so 10,000 clients do not retry in lockstep and flatten a recovering server (a "retry storm"). Stripe and AWS SDKs document exponential backoff with jitter.

interface RetryPolicy { long delayMs(int attempt); } // attempt starts at 1
class Exponential implements RetryPolicy {
    public long delayMs(int a) { return Math.min(10_000, 200L << (a - 1)); }
}

Everyday analogy. A GPS app letting you pick fastest, shortest or avoid tolls: same map, different algorithm.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Strategy is "just inheritance". It is composition: the context holds a strategy, which can change at runtime.
  • Forgetting statelessness: a strategy shared across threads should be immutable or thread-safe.

notes.title: When NOT to use Strategy
notes.html:
Do not reach for it when:

  • There are two variants and no sign of a third. A boolean parameter is simpler. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It).
  • The variants are different in data, not behaviour. Use a config table or enum with fields: enum Tax { GST(0.18), VAT(0.20) }.
  • The choice happens once at startup and never changes. A constructor argument or DI binding is enough; you do not need a setter.
  • The behaviours share so much code that variants are 2-line differences. Then Template Method (next section) or a parameter fits better.

Cost to name. Each strategy is a class (or lambda), plus a place that selects it. For 3 variants that is about 3 extra files in Java, about 3 lines in Kotlin. Debugging jumps through an interface: "which implementation ran?" needs a breakpoint.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-engineering a toy: "I would make a StringUpperCaseStrategy." Resist.
  • Not knowing the lambda form. In Java 8+ and Kotlin, a one-method strategy is a lambda.

notes.title: Template Method: the idea
notes.html:
Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses fill in specific steps. The base class controls the order ("don't call us, we'll call you"); subclasses override only the varying steps.

Good fit: the steps are always the same sequence, only a few steps differ. Examples: data import (open, parse, validate, save, close), report generation, game turn, test lifecycle.

+------------------------------+
| abstract DataImporter        |
| + run()   <-- final template |
|   open(); parse(); validate();|
|   save(); close();           |
| # parse()    abstract        |
| # validate() hook (default)  |
+--------------+---------------+
               ^
      +--------+---------+
      |                  |
 CsvImporter        JsonImporter

Before: two classes copy-pasted the open/validate/save/close code and differ only in parse. A bug fixed in one (say, forgetting to close the file) stays alive in the other.

After:

abstract class DataImporter {
    public final void run(String path) {          // final: order cannot be broken
        open(path);
        try {
            List<Row> rows = parse();             // varies
            if (validate(rows)) save(rows);       // hook with default
        } finally { close(); }                    // always runs
    }
    protected abstract List<Row> parse();
    protected boolean validate(List<Row> rows) { return !rows.isEmpty(); } // hook
    protected void open(String p) { /* shared */ }
    protected void save(List<Row> r) { /* shared */ }
    protected void close() { /* shared */ }
}
class CsvImporter extends DataImporter {
    protected List<Row> parse() { /* split by comma */ return List.of(); }
}

Kotlin variant.

abstract class DataImporter {
    fun run(path: String) {            // not open -> cannot be overridden
        open(path)
        try {
            val rows = parse()
            if (validate(rows)) save(rows)
        } finally { close() }
    }
    protected abstract fun parse(): List<Row>
    protected open fun validate(rows: List<Row>) = rows.isNotEmpty()
    private fun open(p: String) {}
    private fun save(r: List<Row>) {}
    private fun close() {}
}

Kotlin classes and methods are final by default, so run is protected from overriding for free; you must write open for hooks.

Decision gravity. Template Method uses inheritance, which is the harder door to walk back: subclasses depend on the base class's step order and protected members (the "fragile base class" problem). Changing the template can silently break every subclass. If you later want to vary two things independently, you will be refactoring into Strategy.

Everyday analogy. A recipe card for "bake a cake": preheat, mix, bake, cool are fixed; the flavour step (chocolate or vanilla) changes.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting final on the template method.
  • Confusing a hook (optional override, has a default) with an abstract step (must override).
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor: the subclass field is not initialised yet.

notes.title: Template Method in real libraries and Android
notes.html:
Where Template Steps you fill in
Android Activity / Fragment lifecycle driven by the framework onCreate, onStart, onResume ...
Android AsyncTask (old) execute() doInBackground, onPostExecute
Android RecyclerView.Adapter binding flow onCreateViewHolder, onBindViewHolder, getItemCount
Android View measure/draw onMeasure, onDraw
Java InputStream read(byte[]) calls abstract read()
Java AbstractList add/iterator built on get(int), size()
JUnit 4 / 5 test run order @Before, @Test, @After
Spring JdbcTemplate open connection, run, close, map errors your row mapper / callback
Servlet HttpServlet service() dispatches doGet, doPost

Worked example (Activity). The system calls onCreate once, onStart and onResume every time the screen comes forward. If you do a 300 ms disk read inside onCreate, the first frame is late (jank above 16 ms per frame at 60 fps). The template tells you where each kind of work belongs; breaking its rules (not calling super.onCreate()) throws SuperNotCalledException.

Template vs Strategy in one line. Template Method varies steps by inheritance (compile time, class level). Strategy varies a whole algorithm by composition (runtime, object level). Modern advice: prefer Strategy or callbacks ("Spring JdbcTemplate + lambda") unless you truly own the framework skeleton.

Everyday analogy. An airline boarding procedure: same order every flight, only the gate and aircraft differ.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming Activity lifecycle is "Observer". It is a Template Method driven by the framework (observers come in via LifecycleObserver).
  • Not calling super in a hook where the base class does vital work.

notes.title: Template Method refactored to Strategy
notes.html:
When subclassing explodes (CsvJsonUtf8Importer, CsvJsonUtf16Importer ...) switch to composition. Same skeleton, but the varying step is injected.

class DataImporter {
    private final Parser parser;                      // the strategy
    DataImporter(Parser p) { this.parser = p; }
    public void run(String path) {
        open(path);
        try { save(parser.parse()); } finally { close(); }
    }
}
interface Parser { List<Row> parse(); }
class DataImporter(private val parse: () -> List<Row>) {
    fun run(path: String) { /* open */ try { /* save */ parse() } finally { /* close */ } }
}

Trade-off table.

Template Method Strategy
Mechanism inheritance composition
Change at runtime no yes
Number of varying parts easy to add hooks, hard to combine each part is its own strategy
Testing need subclass or mock subclass inject a fake
Coupling base-subclass tight interface-only

Everyday analogy. Template = a franchise with fixed store layout and a local manager. Strategy = the same store plugging in whichever supplier you choose.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "always prefer composition" without noting that Template Method is still ideal for framework hooks you do not own.
  • Stating that one is "better". The answer is when: fixed skeleton owned by you -> Template; swappable algorithm -> Strategy.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Behavioral patterns replace conditionals with polymorphism or add indirection between objects.
  • Strategy: same job, interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, picked at runtime. A lambda in Java 8+/Kotlin when it has one method.
  • Use Strategy for growing variants (discount, retry, comparator); skip it for two stable branches or pure data differences.
  • Template Method: base class fixes the order (final template), subclasses fill abstract steps and optional hooks. Android lifecycle, RecyclerView.Adapter, Spring templates are real cases.
  • Template uses inheritance (fragile base class, compile-time); Strategy uses composition (runtime, testable). Refactor Template to Strategy when subclasses multiply.
  • Always show the before (if/else or copy-paste) and the after in interviews, and say what the pattern costs.
